title: The Well-Stocked Low-Resource Classroom
brief: Open by reframing scarcity as a starting point rather than a deficit. Draw on the source's repeated premise that activities can be completed with very few materials — specifically the create-to-communicate source's statement that 'drawing can be done with very few materials.' Establish the three core assets available in almost any classroom: a board (chalkboard or whiteboard), the students themselves, and improvised or hand-made materials. List the minimal drawing materials named in the source (pencil or pen, paper or chalkboard surface) as a concrete illustration of how little is actually required to run a productive activity. Set the encouraging tone the scope calls for by emphasising that constraints define a starting point for creative planning, not a ceiling on quality teaching.

title: Drawing Activities: The Board and Beyond
brief: Focus entirely on drawing as a zero-budget classroom tool, drawing exclusively on the create-to-communicate source. Cover the two drawing modes described there — drawing from observation (food, plants, animals, household objects, local landscapes) and drawing from imagination — and explain the practical tip the source gives for both: breaking any subject into basic shapes to build an outline before adding detail. Emphasise the source's explicit reassurance that with imaginative drawing 'there is no right or wrong way,' and explain how this lowers affective barriers. Connect drawing to the language goals the source names: reinforcing vocabulary, practising grammatical structures, and generating oral conversation. Show how the chalkboard or whiteboard itself serves as the drawing surface when paper is unavailable, using the source's own list of required versus optional materials.

title: Students as the Material: Pair and Group Work
brief: Show how the students themselves are the richest resource in a low-budget classroom by focusing on pair and group work formats described across the shaping_frm_observ source. Draw on the source's references to pair work (e.g., the Mad Lib activity completed 'in pairs or small groups'), peer assessment worksheets, and self-assessment checklists to illustrate that structured student-to-student interaction requires no equipment. Cover the self- and peer editing stations described in the Unit 12 supplementary resources — the source explains that students use a checklist to assess their own writing and to get feedback from peers — as a model of a fully student-resourced activity. Also draw on the source's mention of the Writing Mechanics Checklist, used by pairs to check and give feedback on each other's writing. Frame these formats as reusable routines that cost nothing once established.

title: Signal Words and Classroom Routines as Structure
brief: Use the source's discussion of signal words from the primary classroom unit to show how consistent verbal or gestural cues replace the need for printed instructions, timers, or technology. The source states that a teacher used a special word ('magic') to indicate the beginning or end of an activity and transition to another activity, and asks what the advantage of using signal words to create routines is. Build from this to explain how routines — predictable sequences that students internalise — reduce the cognitive overhead of managing a class with limited materials. Draw also on the source's reference to hand, arm, or body movements that correspond to words in songs, poems, or stories as another no-cost routine device. Present signal words and movement routines as tools that turn the absence of equipment into an asset: when transitions are smooth and predictable, lesson momentum is maintained without relying on any technology.

title: Improvised Materials: Puppets, Pocket Books, and Graphic Organizers
brief: Survey the hand-made and improvised material types described in the shaping_frm_observ supplementary resources to give teachers a concrete menu of options. Cover flip books (the source lists materials and step-by-step instructions), full-sized paper puppets, hand puppets, and stick puppets — all described as makeable from basic supplies. Include pocket books ('What Do I See?' and 'The Book About Me') as examples of student-made reading and writing materials. Introduce the K-W-L Chart graphic organizer, which the source describes as usable as a warm-up activity with a reflection follow-up, encouraging learners to think about what they know, what they want to know, and what they have learned — and note that the source explicitly states teachers can reproduce it on the board, making paper optional. Present the Brainstorming graphic organizer the same way. Frame all of these as templates teachers can draw once on the board and reuse across many lessons.

title: Mini-Projects as a Routine End Product
brief: Show how project-based learning can function as a recurring, low-resource lesson structure by drawing on the shaping_frm_observ source's descriptions of mini-projects. The source lists concrete student outputs that require no technology: role-plays, presentations, written stories, and posters. Draw on the Project Checklist: Learning New Vocabulary resource described in the source — a checklist that guides small groups through preparing a presentation using new vocabulary, with a self-assessment rubric for students and a teacher's rubric included — as a model of a structured project that needs only paper and a board. Reference the source's advice to include options for both individual and collaborative work and to create a defined end product or performance outcome. Close by connecting mini-projects to the unit's core theme: when the end product is a student performance or a hand-made poster, the constraint of having no technology becomes irrelevant, and the routine of working toward a visible outcome motivates students lesson after lesson.
